questions.q: Name the five founding leaders of NAM and the year and venue of the first NAM Summit.
questions.a: The five founding leaders were Jawaharlal Nehru (India), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Sukarno (Indonesia), and Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana). The first NAM Summit was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in September 1961. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Nasser but missing Tito, or citing 1955 Bandung as the first summit) reveals confusion between the Bandung Conference (precursor) and the formal NAM launch, and ignorance of Yugoslavia's unique position as a European communist state outside the Warsaw Pact.

questions.q: Explain why the 1955 Bandung Conference is considered the ideological precursor to NAM, and list any three of the Ten Principles of Bandung.
questions.a: The 1955 Bandung Conference brought together 29 newly independent Asian and African nations to assert their collective voice against colonialism and great-power rivalry. It articulated the Ten Principles (Dasasila Bandung) — including respect for sovereignty, non-interference, equality, peaceful settlement of disputes, and promotion of mutual cooperation — which became NAM's founding charter. A wrong answer that treats Bandung as merely a "meeting of Asian countries" or lists NATO/Warsaw Pact principles instead shows failure to grasp the anti-colonial, South-South solidarity core of NAM's ideology.

questions.q: India signed the 1971 Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with the Soviet Union. Critics argue this violated NAM's non-alignment principle. Using the concept of "strategic autonomy," evaluate whether this treaty was a betrayal of non-alignment or a pragmatic exercise of it.
questions.a: The 1971 treaty was a pragmatic exercise of strategic autonomy, not a betrayal. Non-alignment meant freedom to choose partners issue-by-issue, not equidistance from both blocs. India faced a clear security threat from a US-Pakistan-China axis (evident in the 1971 Bangladesh crisis), while the USSR offered diplomatic cover and military supplies without demanding base rights or ideological conformity. The treaty had no mutual defence clause (unlike NATO/Warsaw Pact). A wrong answer calling it "alignment with USSR" confuses non-alignment with neutrality; neutrality implies passivity, non-alignment implies active, independent judgment — a distinction Nehru explicitly made in his 1961 Belgrade speech.

questions.q: Compare NAM's stance on nuclear disarmament with that of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). Why did NAM countries (including India) refuse to sign the NPT in 1968?
questions.a: NAM demanded universal, non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament — linking non-proliferation to disarmament by nuclear-weapon states. The NPT created a two-tier system: nuclear "haves" (US, USSR, UK, France, China) could keep arsenals while "have-nots" were permanently barred. NAM viewed this as "nuclear apartheid" violating the Bandung Principle of sovereign equality. India's 1974 Pokhran test and 1998 tests were assertions of this principle. A wrong answer that says "India wanted nuclear weapons" misses the normative argument: NAM opposed the NPT's structural inequality, not non-proliferation per se.

questions.q: Assess the criticism that "NAM was irrelevant during the Cold War because it could not prevent superpower interventions in member states (e.g., Soviet invasion of Afghanistan 1979, US interventions in Latin America)."
questions.a: The criticism confuses NAM's normative influence with enforcement power. NAM lacked military capacity — by design, it rejected military alliances. Its relevance lay in: (a) providing a diplomatic platform for decolonisation (NAM pressure accelerated independence in Angola, Mozambique, Namibia); (b) shaping UN agenda (NAM caucus passed key resolutions on New International Economic Order, apartheid); (c) creating "strategic space" for members to manoeuvre between blocs. The 1979 Havana Summit's divided vote on Afghanistan (56 supported condemnation, 9 opposed, 26 abstained) showed NAM's internal diversity, not irrelevance. A wrong answer measuring NAM by "did it stop superpowers?" applies a realist metric to a normative project.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word position paper for a hypothetical 2024 NAM Summit arguing whether NAM should (a) dissolve having lost its Cold War purpose, or (b) reinvent itself around climate justice, vaccine equity, and UN Security Council reform.
questions.a: A strong paper will: (1) acknowledge the original bipolar context is gone; (2) argue NAM's core principle — collective autonomy of the Global South — remains valid because power asymmetry persists (G7 vs G77); (3) propose concrete reinvention: climate finance as new "disarmament" agenda, technology transfer as new "decolonisation," UNSC expansion as new "sovereign equality"; (4) cite NAM's 120 members (2/3 of UN) as institutional capital. A weak paper either romanticises 1961 nostalgia or adopts Western "NAM is dead" talking points without analysing current Global South demands (e.g., BRICS expansion, G20 presidency rotation).
